lesson.4_1.title: Loans and EMIs
lesson.4_1.gut.prompt: A phone costs ₹6,000. The shop offers a "no-cost EMI": 6 payments of ₹1,000. Or you can wait 3 months and pay ₹5,500 in cash. What do you do?
lesson.4_1.gut.bridge: Borrowing has a price. Let's learn the words that show it.
lesson.4_1.gut.a.label: Take the EMI today
lesson.4_1.gut.a.result: You get the phone now and pay ₹6,000 in all. That is ₹500 more than the cash price.
lesson.4_1.gut.b.label: Wait and pay cash
lesson.4_1.gut.b.result: No phone for 3 months. Then you pay ₹5,500 and owe nothing.
lesson.4_1.gut.c.label: Ask what "no-cost" really means
lesson.4_1.gut.c.result: Good question. The cost is hiding in the ₹500 cash discount you would give up.
lesson.4_1.c1.text: Borrowing lets you have something now and pay later. "Later" always has a price.
lesson.4_1.c2.text: A loan is money you borrow and must pay back. The amount you borrow is the principal.
lesson.4_1.c3.text: The lender charges an interest rate: a percent of what you owe, for each year. The time you take to repay is the tenure.
lesson.4_1.c4.text: An EMI is the fixed amount you pay every month. Each EMI pays some interest and some of the principal.
lesson.4_1.c4.reveal.prompt: Borrow ₹6,000 at 18% a year for 6 months. What is the EMI?
lesson.4_1.c4.reveal.answer: About ₹1,053 a month. Six of them add up to about ₹6,319, so the loan costs about ₹319.
lesson.4_1.c5.text: A flat rate charges interest on the full amount for the whole time, even as you repay. A reducing rate charges only on what you still owe.
lesson.4_1.c5.reveal.prompt: "Flat 9% for a year" sounds small. What is it really?
lesson.4_1.c5.reveal.answer: About 16% a year on the money you still owe.
lesson.4_1.c6.text: Lenders may charge a processing fee at the start. A "no-cost EMI" can hide its cost in a cash discount you lose.
lesson.4_1.c6.sort.prompt: Does it add to the cost of borrowing?
lesson.4_1.c6.sort.discount: A cash discount you give up
lesson.4_1.c6.sort.feedback: The cost of a loan is everything you pay beyond the amount you borrowed.
lesson.4_1.c7.text: Always compare the total you will repay with the price today.
lesson.4_1.q1.prompt: Which number shows the real cost of a loan?
lesson.4_1.q1.right: Yes. Total repaid minus the amount borrowed is what the loan cost you.
lesson.4_1.q1.wrong: A small EMI can hide a big cost. Add up everything you repay, then subtract what you borrowed.
lesson.4_1.q1.o2: The total you repay minus what you borrowed
lesson.4_1.q2.prompt: A "no-cost EMI" never costs anything extra.
lesson.4_1.q2.right: Correct, it's false. The cost can sit in a lost cash discount or a fee.
lesson.4_1.q2.wrong: It's false. Compare the total of the EMIs with the cash price. The gap is the cost.
lesson.4_1.q3.prompt: Two loans of ₹6,000 for one year. One says "flat 9%". One says "9% reducing". Which costs more?
lesson.4_1.q3.right: Right. A flat rate keeps charging on the full amount, even after you have repaid part of it.
lesson.4_1.q3.wrong: The flat loan costs more. It charges interest on the full ₹6,000 all year, even as you repay.
lesson.4_1.effect: You can now take a loan. A loan adds a liability, and its EMI leaves your wallet every month before anything else.
lesson.4_2.title: Credit cards and Buy-Now-Pay-Later
lesson.4_2.gut.prompt: You owe ₹4,000 on a credit card. The bill says "Minimum due: ₹200". What do you pay?
lesson.4_2.gut.bridge: A card is borrowed money with its own words. Let's read them.
lesson.4_2.gut.a.label: Pay the ₹200 minimum
lesson.4_2.gut.a.result: You avoid a late fee. But ₹3,800 is still owed, and interest is charged on it.
lesson.4_2.gut.b.label: Pay the full ₹4,000
lesson.4_2.gut.b.result: Nothing is left for the bank to charge interest on.
lesson.4_2.gut.c.label: Pay ₹2,000
lesson.4_2.gut.c.result: More than the minimum. Interest is still charged on the ₹2,000 that is left.
lesson.4_2.c1.text: A debit card spends your own money. A credit card spends the bank's money, and you repay it.
lesson.4_2.c2.text: The credit limit is the most you can borrow on the card.
lesson.4_2.c3.text: Each month is a billing cycle. Then a bill arrives with a due date. Pay the whole bill by that date and you pay no interest. That gap is the interest-free period.
lesson.4_2.c4.text: The bill also shows a minimum due: the smallest payment that avoids a late fee. Pay only that, and interest is charged on the rest.
lesson.4_2.c4.reveal.prompt: Does paying the minimum due clear your debt?
lesson.4_2.c4.reveal.answer: No. It only avoids the late fee. What is left keeps growing with interest.
lesson.4_2.c5.text: Buy-Now-Pay-Later is borrowing too. Small payments are easy to forget, and a missed one brings a fee.
lesson.4_2.c5.sort.feedback: If someone else pays first and you repay later, it is borrowing.
lesson.4_2.c6.text: How much of your limit you use is called utilisation. Lenders look at it when they judge you.
lesson.4_2.q1.prompt: What does paying only the minimum due do?
lesson.4_2.q1.right: Yes. The minimum keeps the late fee away. The debt is still there, with interest.
lesson.4_2.q1.wrong: The minimum only avoids the late fee. Interest is charged on everything you did not pay.
lesson.4_2.q1.o2: It avoids the late fee, but interest is charged on the rest
lesson.4_2.q2.right: Correct, it's false. Someone pays for you now and you repay later. That is borrowing.
lesson.4_2.q2.wrong: It's false. If you repay later, you borrowed, even when the payments are small.
lesson.4_2.q3.prompt: Your card's limit is ₹10,000 and you have used ₹3,000. What is your utilisation?
lesson.4_2.q3.wrong: Utilisation is what you used divided by your limit: ₹3,000 ÷ ₹10,000 = 30%.
lesson.4_2.effect: You decide whether to check your credit score. Checking it for the first time starts your credit profile.
lesson.4_3.title: Credit score
lesson.4_3.gut.prompt: Two students ask a bank for the same ₹6,000 loan. One has a credit score of 760. The other has 590. What happens?
lesson.4_3.gut.bridge: Your record becomes a number. Here is how it works.
lesson.4_3.gut.a.label: Both get the same loan
lesson.4_3.gut.a.result: No. A lender prices each person by their record.
lesson.4_3.gut.b.label: 760 gets a cheaper loan; 590 is refused
lesson.4_3.gut.b.result: Yes. In this game a score of 760 is offered up to ₹10,000 at 14% a year. Under 600, banks decline.
lesson.4_3.gut.c.label: 590 gets the bigger loan
lesson.4_3.gut.c.result: No. A lower score means a smaller and costlier offer, or none at all.
lesson.4_3.c1.text: A lender cannot see your character. It looks at your record of repaying.
lesson.4_3.c2.text: A credit score is a number that shows how reliably you repay. In this game it runs from 300 to 900.
lesson.4_3.c3.text: You have no score until you first use credit. In this game you then start at 650.
lesson.4_3.c4.text: What moves it up: paying every EMI on time, and finishing a loan on schedule.
lesson.4_3.c4.reveal.prompt: In this game, what does one on-time EMI do?
lesson.4_3.c4.reveal.answer: It adds 10 points. Finishing a loan on schedule adds 15 more.
lesson.4_3.c5.text: What pulls it down: a missed payment, using most of your limit, and many loan applications at once.
lesson.4_3.c5.sort.prompt: Does it push the score up or down?
lesson.4_3.c5.sort.many: Applied for three loans in one month
lesson.4_3.c5.sort.feedback: In this game a missed EMI costs 40 points and a ₹200 late fee.
lesson.4_3.c6.text: Your score decides the rate and the amount a lender offers. In this game: 750 and above, up to ₹10,000 at 14%. 700 to 749, up to ₹8,000 at 18%. 650 to 699, up to ₹6,000 at 22%. 600 to 649, up to ₹3,000 at 26%. Under 600, banks decline.
lesson.4_3.c7.text: The same ₹6,000 for 6 months: the EMI is ₹1,041 at 14% and ₹1,065 at 22%. A good record makes borrowing cheaper.
lesson.4_3.q1.prompt: Which action raises a credit score?
lesson.4_3.q1.right: Yes. Paying on time, every time, is what builds a score.
lesson.4_3.q1.wrong: A score rises when you repay on time. Missed payments and many applications pull it down.
lesson.4_3.q1.o2: Applying for many loans in one month
lesson.4_3.q2.prompt: A higher credit score can get you a lower interest rate.
lesson.4_3.q2.right: Correct. Lenders offer a lower rate to people with a strong record.
lesson.4_3.q2.wrong: It's true. A strong record means the lender takes less risk, so it charges less.
lesson.4_3.q3.prompt: You have never borrowed anything. What is your credit score?
lesson.4_3.q3.right: Right. A score only exists once there is a record to score.
lesson.4_3.q3.wrong: With no borrowing there is no record, so there is no score yet.
lesson.4_3.q3.o2: You do not have one yet
lesson.4_3.effect: Your credit score meter appears. From now on, the rate and the maximum of any loan offer depend on it.
lesson.4_4.title: Formal and informal borrowing
lesson.4_4.gut.prompt: A friend asks you to co-sign a ₹5,000 loan. What are you agreeing to?
lesson.4_4.gut.bridge: Where you borrow matters as much as how much.
lesson.4_4.gut.a.label: Saying they are a good person
lesson.4_4.gut.a.result: It is more than that. A co-signer must pay if the borrower does not.
lesson.4_4.gut.b.label: Paying the loan if they do not
lesson.4_4.gut.b.result: Right. Their missed payment becomes your debt, and it can hurt your credit score.
lesson.4_4.c1.text: Money can be borrowed from many places. They do not all play by the same rules.
lesson.4_4.c2.text: A bank or an NBFC is a regulated lender. There are rules, receipts and somewhere to complain.
lesson.4_4.c3.text: A moneylender or an unknown loan app works outside those rules. The rate can be very high and there may be no paper trail.
lesson.4_4.c3.reveal.prompt: 10% a month sounds small. What is that over a year?
lesson.4_4.c3.reveal.answer: About 120% a year. On ₹2,800 that is ₹280 every month in interest alone.
lesson.4_4.c4.text: Some loan apps ask for your contacts and photos. They can use them to pressure you if you pay late.
lesson.4_4.c4.sort.fast: Money in two minutes, no questions
lesson.4_4.c4.sort.feedback: A lender that hides its terms, or wants your contacts, is one to walk away from.
lesson.4_4.c5.text: Before you borrow, check that the lender is regulated. The RBI lists approved digital lending apps, and its Sachet portal takes complaints.
lesson.4_4.c6.text: A lender may ask for collateral: something it can take if you do not pay. Or for a co-signer: someone who must pay if you do not.
lesson.4_4.q1.prompt: What does a co-signer agree to?
lesson.4_4.q1.right: Yes. A co-signer carries the debt if the borrower stops paying.
lesson.4_4.q1.wrong: A co-signer is not a reference. They owe the money if the borrower does not pay.
lesson.4_4.q1.o2: To repay the loan if the borrower does not
lesson.4_4.q2.prompt: A loan app that asks for your contact list is a normal, safe sign.
lesson.4_4.q2.right: Correct, it's false. Lending does not need your contacts. It is a warning sign.
lesson.4_4.q2.wrong: It's false. A lender has no need for your contacts. Some use them to pressure borrowers.
lesson.4_4.q3.prompt: Which of these lenders must follow the regulator's rules?
lesson.4_4.q3.right: Right. A bank is regulated: it has rules to follow and you have somewhere to complain.
lesson.4_4.q3.wrong: A bank is the regulated one. The other two work outside those rules.
lesson.4_4.q3.o2: A loan app that is not on the regulator's list
lesson.4_4.effect: When you next borrow, you choose the lender. The total cost of each choice is shown before you decide.
